title: Malaysia’s governor asks what ASEAN’s Islamic finance growth has actually funded
summary: In Manila, Governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour made the case that the next stage of ASEAN Islamic finance should be judged by the businesses, livelihoods and investment it supports. The scale is already considerable. The accompanying presentation puts ASEAN Islamic financial assets at US$1.068 trillion in 2025, up from US$468 billion in 2014, a compound annual increase of 7.8%. More than 180 Islamic banking and takaful institutions operate across six jurisdictions. The governor uses these figures to establish the system’s capacity. They give no measure of how much additional productive investment resulted.

Malaysia developed Islamic finance alongside conventional finance. The governor identifies four conditions that made wider participation possible: legal and tax arrangements that allow fair competition, credible Shariah oversight, connected funding and insurance markets, and the skills and trust needed to make the products work. In the presentation, financial infrastructure includes both a sukuk market and instruments for short-term liquidity management. Even an issuer with a viable long-term project needs intermediaries and investors capable of managing their own liquidity. For customers, transparent terms, fair treatment and competitive pricing influence whether a formally available product is used.

Malaysia’s iTEKAD programme gives his clearest example of the difference between financing and outcomes. It combines seed funding from donations or zakat, microfinance provided by financial institutions and business training. More than 15,000 microentrepreneurs had received support by June 2026. The slide on outcomes separately identifies 5,096 graduates and presents results for a sample of graduates, including an increase in monthly sales for 92% and 2,400 new jobs. Those numbers have different denominators. There is no comparison group, follow-up duration or evidence establishing what participants would have achieved without the combination of funding and training.

At sovereign scale, the governor compares two transactions. The Philippines’ first sovereign sukuk in 2023 raised US$1 billion, with peak demand around 4.9 times the issue size. Malaysia’s US$1.5 billion global sukuk in 2026 priced at the tightest spreads yet achieved for its global sukuk. The first figure measures orders relative to the amount offered; the second describes pricing against Malaysia’s own issuance history. Both suggest access to international capital. Neither establishes what either borrower would have paid for a conventional bond with the same currency, tenor and pricing date.

The regional opportunities he identifies include infrastructure, energy transition, climate resilience and trade finance for halal supply chains. He illustrates bilateral cooperation through a Malaysian bank and a takaful operator already active in the Philippine market, and an Islamic finance qualification developed with the Philippine central bank. He also previews a memorandum with Governor Remolona. These existing activities, and the separately announced agreement, operate at different stages of implementation. The speech presents a case for connecting investors with projects and firms across borders. It specifies no new financing target or guarantee for any individual project.

questions.question: Did the sovereign sukuk attract investors or pricing unavailable in the conventional market?
questions.detail: The Philippine order book and Malaysia’s record spread measure different attributes of two offerings three years apart. Compare each sovereign’s same-currency conventional curve, secondary performance, tenor and final allocations on or around its own pricing date. That would help separate demand for the sukuk structure from the issuer’s general credit standing and the global interest-rate environment.

questions.question: Which part of iTEKAD strengthens businesses after the initial support ends?
questions.detail: The speech associates graduation with better sales, savings and employment, but the cited sample excludes some recipients and has no comparison group. Look for entry conditions, cohort sizes, programme costs and subsequent business survival, alongside comparable applicants who did not receive the same package. Those records would help assess whether adding training and grants changes the repayment capacity of microfinance borrowers.

questions.question: What limits the next cross-border financing transaction?
questions.detail: The governor points to legal frameworks, market liquidity, skills and public trust. A regional asset total cannot identify which constraint matters for a Philippine issuer or a Malaysian intermediary. Study actual sukuk documentation, hedging and liquidity arrangements, market-entry approvals and take-up. This would show where additional institutional cooperation can narrow funding costs or widen access for a viable project.
